title: Bài sưu tầm 111 - Passage 1: Ambergris: Floating Gold of the Oceans
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 111

Ambergris: Floating Gold of the Oceans

Paragraph 1. For thousands of years, beachcombers along the coastlines of the Atlantic and Indian Oceans occasionally stumbled upon a strange, pungent substance cast up by the tide. Variously resembling weathered stone, dense wax, or petrified mud, this enigmatic material was known as ambergris. Long before naturalists understood its biological origin, ancient civilizations attributed mystical properties to the substance. Arab merchants believed it welled up from subterranean springs beneath the sea floor, while Chinese folklore claimed it was the solidified saliva of coastal dragons. Despite its repulsive initial appearance, ambergris became one of the most lucrative trading commodities in the ancient world, treasured across continents as a medicinal panacea, an aphrodisiac, and an irreplaceable fixative in luxury perfumery.

Paragraph 2. The true biological source of ambergris was only confirmed in the nineteenth century with the expansion of commercial whaling. The substance is produced exclusively within the digestive tract of the sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus). Sperm whales are deep-diving predators whose primary diet consists of colossal and giant squid. While the whale’s stomach enzymes easily digest the cephalopods’ soft flesh, the hard, razor-sharp chitinous beaks of the squid cannot be dissolved. Normally, the whale regurgitates these indigestible remnants. Occasionally, however, fragments bypass the stomach and lodge in the lower intestine, irritating the delicate mucosa. In response to this internal trauma, the whale’s gall bladder secretes an oily, cholesterol-rich bile compound to encase the sharp beaks, gradually forming a dense, compact mass.

Paragraph 3. Over time, this obstruction accumulates layers of organic matter, eventually forming an enormous boulder-like lump inside the animal. While early biologists assumed the creature always died from intestinal rupture, contemporary marine autopsies suggest that the mass is frequently passed out naturally into the ocean through defecation. When first voided into the water, raw ambergris is soft, dark black, and emits an overwhelming stench of rotting feces. To become commercially valuable, it must undergo decades of oceanic curing. Floating buoyantly on the surface of the sea, the mass is subjected to the relentless bleaching of salt water and direct sunlight. Over years or even centuries of marine drift, photochemical oxidation breaks down organic impurities, transforming the substance into a light grey or silvery-white stone with a firm, waxy texture. In this cured state, its offensive odour softens into a rich, sweet, and subtly earthy fragrance.

Paragraph 4. The extraordinary commercial value of cured ambergris—often fetching prices exceeding $20,000 per kilogram—lies in a unique chemical constituent called ambrein. While ambrein itself is practically scentless, it possesses the remarkable physical property of binding to volatile aroma molecules. In luxury perfumes, botanical extracts and citrus oils evaporate rapidly when applied to warm human skin. When dissolved in alcohol alongside tiny quantities of ambrein, these transient top-notes are chemically stabilized, allowing the fragrance to endure on the skin for hours or days without altering its delicate aromatic profile. Beyond perfumery, historical records document that King Charles II of England enjoyed ambergris as a culinary delicacy, routinely eating it grated over breakfast eggs.

Paragraph 5. In modern times, the international commerce of ambergris is legally complex. In the United States, the Endangered Species Act strictly bans the possession, import, or sale of any product derived from sperm whales, even naturally shed beach finds. Conversely, in the United Kingdom and the European Union, ambergris found washed up on shore is classified as biological waste and salvage, making private collection and commercial auction entirely legal. While industrial chemists have successfully developed synthetic alternatives such as ambroxan to supply mass-market cosmetics, master perfumers maintain that no chemical substitute can replicate the complex, multifaceted warmth of genuine natural ambergris.

q8.text: Scientists in the nineteenth century discovered the true origin of ambergris through commercial whaling.

steps: Đoạn 2: "The true biological source of ambergris was only confirmed in the nineteenth century with the expansion of commercial whaling."

q9.text: Most sperm whales die from internal injuries caused by the buildup of ambergris.

steps: Đoạn 3: "...contemporary marine autopsies suggest that the mass is frequently passed out naturally into the ocean through defecation." → Mâu thuẫn trực tiếp với việc hầu hết cá voi chết vì chấn thương bên trong.

q10.text: The chemical compound ambrein produces a powerful fragrance on its own.

steps: Đoạn 4: "While ambrein itself is practically scentless..." → Mâu thuẫn với produces a powerful fragrance.

q11.text: European law treats ambergris found on shore as an illegal animal product.

steps: Đoạn 5: "...in the United Kingdom and the European Union, ambergris found washed up on shore is classified as biological waste and salvage, making private collection and commercial auction entirely legal." → Hợp pháp, không phải bất hợp pháp.

q12.text: Synthetic chemicals have completely replaced natural ambergris in all modern luxury perfumes.

steps: Đoạn 5: "...master perfumers maintain that no chemical substitute can replicate the complex, multifaceted warmth of genuine natural ambergris." → Vẫn được các nhà pha chế nước hoa cao cấp dùng, chưa bị thay thế hoàn toàn.

q13.text: High-grade white ambergris is easier to locate on beaches than darker varieties.
